title: Strangler fig, sidecar and ambassador: changing a system that is running

videos.script: Most architecture work is not designing a new system. It is changing one that is running, that customers are using right now, and that cannot stop while you work on it. {{running}} The tempting plan is to write the new system beside the old one and switch over on a chosen day. That plan has a long record of failing. {{rewrite}} This lesson is about the alternative, which replaces a system one piece at a time while it keeps serving. Martin Fowler named it after a fig tree that grows around another until it stands on its own. {{fig}} On your machine you will take the stock module out of Quitanda's monolith, without changing a single request a client sends: first a tenth of the traffic, then all of it, with a way back at every step. {{strangle}} Then two patterns that put a small program beside a service to do work the service should not have to. A sidecar, beside the stock service, sees every request coming in. {{sidecar}} An ambassador, beside the monolith, handles every call going out to a payment gateway that is often busy. {{ambassador}} They are the same program in the lab, and the lesson shows why where it sits is the whole difference.
